speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Explain.

There are two changes contemplated in the proposed bill. The first is to amend paragraph (b), subsection 3, of section 25, and would empower the minister to purchase silver for the redemption of dominion notes. The second amendment is to repeal subsection 4 of section 26. As the section stands at present, it expressly prohibits the Bank of Canada from purchasing a greater amount of silver than 1,671,802. fine ounces during a period of three years- 1935, 1936 and 1937. The change proposed in the bill provides that the Bank of Canada shall not hold less than 1,671,802 fine ounces and so removes the prohibitory provision of the section.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO HERO OF VIMY AND FORMER
subsubtopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL BY MR. BENNETT, MR. MACKENZIE KING AND MR. GARDINER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
members of both houses of parliament and the people of Canada generally will greatly appreciate the tribute which has just been paid by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to the memory of the late Lord Byng. As leader of the opposition and one who for a number of years enjoyed the closest official and personal relations with Lord Byng, may I say in depp sincerity that I join with all that has been said in praise of the great career which has just drawn to its close, and of the qualities which won for Lord Byng in his lifetime not only the admiration but the abiding regard and esteem of those who served with him and of all who knew him best. The loss which Britain mourns to-day in the passing of one of her most distinguished sons is a loss which will be felt in all parts of the British empire, but in no other part as much as in this dominion. Because of his immediate contact with Canadians in the great war as commander of the Canadian corps, and of the high position he held in Canada as governor general, Lord Byng was brought, on the field of battle and in affairs of state, into closer association with a larger number of Canadians than any other person who has held either of those positions. In that twofold way his life was more intimately linked with the lives of many of our people than that of any other governor general.
I shall not attempt to review the career of the late Lord Byng; that has already been done by the Prime Minister, and indeed it is already a part of history itself. But I should like to join with the Prime Minister in giving expression to a thought or two arising out of the personal association which I was privileged to have with Lord Byng during the years that I enjoyed the intimate and close association to which I have referred. Of the many qualities which served to endear Lord Byng to those who knew him I should say the greatest of all was his ever present sense of duty. Viewing hia life as a whole, one cannot but see in it much that, from the point of view of service to the crown and to the state, was exemplary. From the very beginning of his interest in affairs it was a life of service, and service in a very large way. That life of service carried with it those characteristics of conscientiousness, fearlessness, love of
The Late Viscount Byng

justice, the desire to see the right thing done, and to further the right with which one associates faithfulness to duty. Another quality which endeared Lord Byng to those who knew him best was his great modesty and accessibility. There was something exceptionally fine in the directness and simplicity of his nature. There was nothing affected about him, he was naturalness itself in his relations with his fellow men. Moreover, by nature, he was genuinely considerate and kind. He had a very great love for his fellow men. I think it was a distinguishing characteristic, that he was particularly fond of the average man. He had an especial concern, naturally, for those who- had served with him in the great war, and it is little wonder that his name is held in reverence by the veterans of that, great struggle. But his sympathy was essentially with human nature andl with men of all classes. That was evidenced while he was in Canada by the extent to which he went from one end of this country to the other to become personally informed and acquainted with conditions, and to meet and know the people. I venture to say there are few, if any, who have held the great office of governor general in Canada who have left behind more personal friends and acquaintances than it was Lord Byng's privilege to have made during the time he was in this country.
There were other qualities, to one of which the Prime Minister has referred, which were also outstanding. Lord Byng was a great friend. I always felt in my association with him during the years I was in office that I had in him a friend with whom' I could discuss most intimately and advantageously all the affairs that came before the government for consideration. The years from 1921 to 1925 were difficult and trying years. I should like to say that throughout that period I constantly felt that the government could not have received from a governor general more helpful counsel and assistance than was sought to be given to my colleagues and myself by Lord Byng.
Perhaps I can best express what my feelings were towards Lord Byng when I say to the house that in the early part of 1926, when we were drawing near to the end of Lord Byng's term of office and it became necessary to recommend a successor, I wrote to the British Prime Minister and said that, so happy and cordial had our relations been in all respects throughout all the time that Lord Byng had heen here and we had shared so fully each others confidence, there was nothing which my colleagues and myself would

more welcome, if it were agreeable to Lord Byng himself and to His Majesty the King, than an extension or renewal of his term of office as governor general. Such was the nature of our official relations. As is known, those official relations were severed owing to a difference of view on, a constitutional question. But I felt then, I feel now, and I shall always feel, as regards both Lord Byng and myself, that each of us, with respect to that particular matter, did that which was right in his own eyes.
I feel that the empire has lost a great soldier, an exemplary citizen and a good man. I think we may all be proud that the name of Lord Byng of Vimy will have an enduring association with our dominion both at home and abroad. I join with the Prime Minister, as my colleagues on this side of the house will wish to do, in his request that Your Honour convey to Lady Byng an expression of the deep sympathy felt for her in her great bereavement by all hon,. members of this House of Commons.

speechtext: It was with deep regret that we learned a few minutes ago of the passing of Lord Byng, former governor general of Canada. Those of us who had the privilege of meeting him here, and indeed citizens resident in different parts of Canada who had that privilege, realize that his most outstanding quality was his broad human sympathy. I join with the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition in extending to his bereaved relatives and to all those who are near and dear to him an expression of deep sympathy with them in their sad loss.

The commission has been in operation only since January 1, 1933, and it was thought that it should be continued a few months longer and we should let another parliament decide whether it should be abolished or its powers modified. A bill will be presented shortly to extend the life of the commission to the end of this fiscal year.

This is the vote under which extension of services will take place. The sendee in British Columbia is

very unsatisfactory and I should like to know what works are to be undertaken to bring about improvements.

I am not in a position to give details but I may say that the commission has in mind the construction of powerful stations throughout Canada, one to be located in Vancouver. The commission hopes to be able to start this program of construction within a very short time.
Is anything provided in this vote for that work?

I understand that the commission intends to use a certain part of this vote to start its program. I believe it intends to commence the construction of the station in Vancouver as soon as it is authorized by the government.

The minister has just indicated that the commission proposes to construct a high-powered station in Vancouver. As briefly as possible I should like to outline the situation in British Columbia. Vancouver and its immediate environments on the lower mainland is situated in the southwest corner of the province and I believe this is one of the reasons why we have such unsatisfactory service. There are six private stations operating in Vancouver and even though -the city and its immediate surroundings contains two-thirds of the population of the province I believe it has pretty fair service at the present time. The government should consider carefully before it decides to construct another high-powered station in Vancouver. The minister should consider if it would not be for the general benefit of the outlying sections of the province to locate such a station at a more central point than the city of Vancouver. The reception received by points in the interior of the province is exceedingly unsatisfactory and the construction of a high-powered station in Vancouver will not improve the situation. One quarter of the power of such a station will go out over the Pacific ocean while another quarter will go south across the line where the American people are well served with their own stations. The people in the interior of the province have no reception at all except when they turn on the American stations. The general complaint throughout the province is that they can only get reception from the American stations. -I therefore appeal to the minister to have this situation looked into carefully and to see whether a 'better location could not be secured than the city of Vancouver.
(Mr. J. A. Fraser.]
I shall ibe pleased to call the attention of the radio commission to my hon. friend's remarks, which I am sure they will consider carefully.
Is it the intention of the commission to discontinue broadcasting French programs in the western provinces?
I have no intimation or knowledge of any such intention on the part of the commission.

It is recognized that Vancouver is the most central point in British Columbia as regards population, and I would impress on the minister the advisability when the station is built of having it sufficiently strong and sufficiently high powered that interior points will be taken care of, especially in tihe riding of Cariboo, from which my hon. friend comes.
What progress has been made in the last year by the commission either in acquiring stations or in building new ones?

I have not the details before me of what they have done in the last twelve months. I know however that the commission has built and opened a station in the city of Quebec and another one, more than a year ago, at Chicoutimi. Another one is in operation at New Carlisle in Bonaventure county, and I believe a station of 1,000 watts was purchased and is operated at Windsor, Ontario. There are other stations which have been opened up by the commission, not very powerful however-1,000 and 5,000 watt stations.
What progress has been made by the commission in talcing care of outlying districts, not only in Quebec but in other parts of Canada, which do not get very much service from the ordinary stations?

The aim of the commission is to cover every section of Canada as far as possible, but as I have already stated the appropriations that have been voted have not been sufficient to allow the commission to build expensive stations such as are built in other countries. The commissioners have been doing all they possibly could with the moneys available, 81,000,000 odd voted last year and the amount being voted this year; but they cannot maintain first class programs and build powerful stations all over Canada in one year. Everyone will admit, I think, that the amount is inadequate, but it was our view that in these years of depression we should not have been justified in asking this house to vote large amounts to build powerful stations

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
When the bill is introduced extending the life of the radio commission until the end of the next fiscal year, as it will be, I desire to make some observations touching the whole radio situation in this dominion. The real truth is that the effort to destroy this publicly owned utility is very well known and is very active, and whether or not the utility can be saved will depend upon the attitude of the House of Commons towards it and their willingness to realize that a country that is as poor as we are cannot spend at once the money that is required to make this facility as perfect as it should be. I may say to this committee very frankly that it will require a very large sum of money to give a country of the size of this that coverage which would approach perfection. I had occasion the other day in England to make some inquiries regarding the manner in which they were proceeding with their broadcasting corporation. It will be known to members of this committee that Sir John Reith, who is managing director of the British Broadcasting Corporation, went to South Africa to make them a report, and he reported-I think the report has been published; if not, I am not divulging any confidence when I say that he reported in favour of a publicly owned service. The same applies to Australia and New Zealand. We in this country are in an exceedingly difficult position. We have ten and a half millions of people and we have to rent several thousands of miles of wire in order to broadcast on an efficient scale. That is very expensive having regard to the existing rates for leasing wires both from railways and telephone 92582-213
companies. And then always insidiously is the attack made against the publicly owned facility and the effort made to destroy it. I will deal with that at somewhat greater length, but I should like to say this to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). Possibly he realizes that sometimes in our anxiety to be critical-I am not referring to anything that has taken place to-day but more to what occurred last year-we do the thing itself an injury. I think that perhaps that is recognized by most men who have studied the situation. I have a considerable amount of information and I shall be pleased to place it before the house on the second reading or when the bill is in committee. I am convinced that at the present time only one of two things can be done. Whoever is on the treasury benches will have to ask parliament for a grant of money to enable these facilities to be provided, if they think the conditions in the country will stand it, or to utilize the revenues to the extent that may be possible, gradually to build the stations necessary-gradually.
That is one in the east, one in the west and one somewhere else, in order that there may be a complete coverage. I do not know how the committee feel about the matter, but the more I see of it and know of it, the more determined I would be, if I were here, that I should not yield this facility to any private enterprise. That is my firm conclusion with respect to the matter. I say that very strongly, and the more I see of the matter, the more convinced I am.
I also realize the committee must take cognizance of the fact that we must proceed gradually or else parliament must be prepared to provide a larger sum of money than we feel we can ask at the moment, in order to give effect to some of the recommendations that were made last year. I should like to ask the tolerance of the committee at the present moment in order that when the bill is moved, they may be presented with such facts as various officials have been able to gather together during the past few months and there may be added to it, such observations as are prompted by the information that I have received, for, as the members of the committee possibly know, a committee has been set up again to consider the broadcasting situation in Great Britain. I think it is headed by the former speaker of the House of Commons, the present Lord Ellsworth. That is my memory; I speak subject to correction in that regard. I shall endeavour to

I regard
the statement made by the Prime Minister as probably one of the most important he has made this year in the house. I can assure him now, in the future as in the past, of my hearty cooperation with him in maintaining the principle of public ownership. My purpose in asking the question was far from being critical as I think you, sir, as chairman of the committee of last year will remember. I wish to know, however, whether the government has taken into consideration a recommendation of the committee for an alteration in the set-up of the personnel of the commission, with a view to eliminating certain, charges and difficulties of management that had become apparent to the committee.
As for the commission's work itself, I have for the greater part of that work a very sincere admiration, and I think the commission on the whole is to be congratulated on what it has succeeded in doing with the meagre funds at its disposal and the technical difficulties under which it operates. But that should not prevent those of us who feel that in this question the whole principle of public ownership may be at stake, in doing all we can to see to it that the recommendations of the committee of last year, in so far as they may be practical and possible, are carried out. We felt those recommendations were calculated to stimulate the character of the commission, to strengthen the principle of public ownership in regard to radio broadcasting and to improve the facilities of the commission. I am glad to hear what the Prime Minister has said, and I am sure the committee will wait with interest a further statement from him when the bill comes down.

I was one of those who were on, the original committee that brought in the report upon which was based the bill establishing a radio commission. I was then and I am still in favour of public ownership of this utility. I also earlier this session made some rather strong criticisms of the way in which the work was carried on. I do not propose to repeat those criticisms to-day, but I do hope when the Prime Minister or the 
Minister of Marine, if he has the matter in charge, discusses the bill, some of the criticisms made at that time in good faith will be answered and that there will be some hope at least that the conditions complained of will be remedied.
Before I sit down I would like to ask a question-and it is called forth by an observation of the Prime Minister himself-with regard to the funds available, whether all the revenues that come from licences, any revenues that may come on the account of the radio commission, are used for radio purposes? If they are not, they ought to be and no complaint should be made that- there is not enough money if all the money that comes in on radio account is not used.
My hon. friend knows the amount of revenue in licence fees.
No, I do not.

Last year we collected, I think, $1,480,000, or around $1,500,000. A small balance was left last year. That is why I am asking the committee to vote an amount of SI .500.000. It covers all the .moneys collected from radio licences.
Was the total revenue spent last year?
The total was spent last year.

Arising out of that very matter, may I ask the minister whether he recollects that before the radio commission was set up, there had been on the part of radio listeners an overpayment in relation, to services of a sum that, I am informed, is in the neighbourhood1 of $1,100,000. It is true that that was placed in consolidated revenue account, but in my opinion-and I feel sure, other members of the committee will agree w'ith me-that money should have been appropriated and placed at the disposal of the commission when it was set up. In that case the commission would certainly have had more ample funds to operate with than it has had in the past.
In the event of the amendment proposing an appropriation by parliament to the extent of $1,000,000 to assist in setting up stations owned by the commission, it should be regarded not as a charge upon the radio users of this year but as a general charge upon all the taxpayers for that account, because of the fact that it has been used on general taxpayers' account instead of going, as it should have gone from the beginning, to improve the facilities for those who paid the fees. There is about $1,000,000 of a surplus. Of course it

went into consolidated revenue account and was expended in the usual way, but that amount should never have been 'regarded as usable for that purpose; it should have been kept for the commission or, rather, should have been turned back to it.

speechtext: The question of funds is of course the vital one. In Great Britain they have now over 7,000.000 licensees, a licence costing substantially S2.50 of our money; it is a little more than that. Of that amount the broadcasting commission has only four shillings and sixpence at its disposal; the rest of it goes to the government. But there you have a compact little island of 40,000,000 people, and you have not any such problems as we have such as cost of wires and costs of leasing wires and things of that sort. To-day in France they are projecting advertisements across the channel throughout England, and also in Germany a high-power station is advertising certain goods that are sold largely in the British islands. The problem with us-
Put up a tariff wall.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is it exactly. The problem with us is one of money and I desire to speak at some length about that, because I am going to be extremely frank with the committee. The life or death of our adventure in the field of public ownership of the radio depends largely upon our willingness to nurse this infant until it can become strong enough to fend for itself. That is the real truth about the matter and to do that means that it has to be fed money. The difficulty is to find the money except from the licence payers. I think we should at this time use for the purposes of the commission all the money that comes from licences; that is my view.

I wonder whether the minister could give us any declaration of his policy in regard to a matter about which I had some correspondence with him.
It is the question of giving authority to his inspectors or some branch of the board to compel people who are running electrical machines that cause interference to remedy the trouble. The board spends considerable money in sending cars throughout the country to locate what is called interference. In British Columbia the minister has some very capable men, one especially; he comes around, being requested to do so, and locates the cause of interference. But he is utterly powerless to do anything to have that source of trouble eliminated. He can go and advise people and plead with them, but that is all. Unfortunately, there are hogs in the world 92582-213J
who are indifferent to any appeal of that kind, and will only pay attention to a direct mandate backed by law. Often the trouble can be so easily eliminated. I tied up the whole radio service of the little town where I live one day by starting a small electric fan in my office, and for political reasons L did not wish to be so highly unpopular. It only cost me about $4 to provide the necessary remedj''. There are people who are totally indifferent to the convenience of anyone but themselves, and who will run little electrical machines, which could easily be fixed to avoid any trouble, but, regardless of the inconvenience they are causing, they refuse to do so. In the case of a power plant and the like the cost might run into a greater amount, perhaps $100, but still there is no reason why even they should not march with the times and not cause trouble to a large number of people who now own radios. In these days, when everything we do or say is regimented, from babies upward or downward, as in the case of Ontario, I think we might well put some teeth in the act and give the inspector or the board power to compel the removal of the grievances to which I have alluded.

There is no doubt that one of the great difficulties of our inspectors is that they have no power over those who operate electrical machines which cause interference. I had a report some time ago from the chief of my department suggesting an amendment to the Canadian Radio* Broadcasting Act which would give authority to the inspectors to order certain amelioration of these machines and to confiscate the machines in case the orders of the inspector are not complied with. This is a delicate question, the government have had it under consideration for some time. Would it be advisable to bring in such legislation at this session?

But it has been under consideration for some months, if not a year or more, and I suggest that now is the time for action, in view of the approach of an election when we shall all want to listen to the radio addresses of the leaders. The minister has agreed that this evil exists, then why not take some action? I think the Scriptures say that now is the accepted time, to-morrow may be too late.

There may be a constitutional question on that point; it is a matter of interfering with the right of operation of private property. For instance, phy-

sicians nearly all have electrical machines in their offices which in some cases cause interference with radio reception.
And oil-burners in furnaces.
Some oil-burners, too, but I am told that it is the machines operated by doctors which are causing most trouble at the present time.

But is it not a fact that often it could be remedied at very slight cost? Some are old-fashioned machines, or machines with defective brushes, I think they are called, which could be readily altered. I suggest that the inspectors should have power to use discretion in these matters, and where people deliberately tell him to go to a warmer place and will do nothing, however small the cost, I think he should have power to compel them. 'Why should the convenience of a large number of people suffer from the miserliness or meanness or dog-in-the-manger attitude of such people?

I am not very familiar with the activities of the radio commission. It may well be that the complaints which have arisen are well-founded; indeed one can scarcely think otherwise since they come from all parts of the country. At the same time I feel it is the duty of this house and of the people to give this commission every possible chance to make good. I am a long way from being a socialist to the degree of wanting all our activities brought under government control. I disagree with many of the propositions which are now being made to control us in the activities of our private lives, but at the same time I believe there are some activities that can be performed1 properly only by the people as a whole represented by their government. Such activities we speak of as natural monopolies. There is no reason why broadcasting should be in the hands of private parties. No private individual or company has any vested right to give this service to the people, it is one of the- things that the government should control. When the proposal was made for a radio commission I gave it my heartiest support, and I am still prepared to give it that support. We can well believe that there are private interests that are doing their best to destroy public ownership in radio broadcasting. To me it would be a disaster if through any fault of the commission, whether it be incapacity from the business point of view, or from motives of partisanship, government control of radio should come into such disrepute among the people that they would want the act which

brought the commission into being repealed. The disaster to my mind would be just as great if it were brought about by undue impatience on the part of the people. We should be willing to give the commission a reasonable time in which to make good. That is not saying that there are not some grievances which should be aired. But while having that in view it is in the interest of the Canadian people to give the commission a fair chance, criticizing them where they should be criticized, but at the same time maintaining our stand for public ownership. If public ownership cannot succeed in connection with radio broadcasting, then I do not see any activity in which it can be successful. I am a public ownership man to the extent at least of believing that these natural monopolies should be held by the people. So as I say I hope that nothing in the activities of the commission itself or of undue impatience on the part of the people with imperfections in the service will tend towards putting the whole matter back into the hands of private owners.
Mr. EULEtR: I agree with a good deal of what the last speaker has said. My complaint originally was that so little progress has been made in the purposes for which the commission was established, that is gradually to eliminate private broadcasting. But I shall not deal with that further at the moment. Can the minister say whether the commission has given any consideration to a complaint which has been made by others as well as myself concerning a certain regulation? I have not the exact wording, but this is what I said a few weeks ago:
Then finally I come to the censorship established by the commission .... Article 90 provides that no broadcasting station may broadcast any statements or suggestions contrary to the expressed purpose of any existing legislation.
If I understand the English language that means that any speaker, we will say during the coming .campaign, who criticizes any legislation now on the statute books will be in danger of imprisonment, perhaps. Surely that is not a fair regulation to maintain. It is perfectly certain that during the coming campaign there will be a great deal of criticism of legislation on the statute books to-day, perhaps some of it placed there by the present government. Surely a member of parliament or anyone else speaking publicly during the campaign should not be exposed to any penalty whatever if he declares himself opposed to any legislation that may now exist. That is the only way in which progress can be made, by criticising that which we have

and correcting it if the people see fit to do so. I believe that regulation should be struck out or altered.

Probably my hon.
friend knows that this section of the regulations has not been put into force in any particular case.
It should not 'be there.

The commission has been very broad and lenient towards any public man who wanted to speak over the radio, to criticize laws, governments or parties. The commission has never interfered. The question of whether or not this section should disappear probably will be considered. Certainly I will direct the matter to the attention of the commission and ascertain whether they intend to put that regulation into force.

Does the minister mean to say that the commission has power to pass a regulation with regard to what may be said over the radio that will stifle the speeches broadcast by every hon. member of this house so that, in order to get our opinions expressed, we will have to rely on the daily newspapers and have those opinions circulated. Does the minister mean to imply that he will speak only to the commission about a matter of such great national importance? It sounds to me like the height of absurdity. The government should amend the regulation.
Of course the commission has some control over the private stations and it has the right to prohibit any defamatory speech, for instance.
That is not what it says.

It says a man may not express any opinion contrary to any legislation we now have on the statute books. I protest against the extreme nature of the regulation. I could understand it if they were empowered to prohibit the broadcasting of speeches of an inflammatory nature, or those which perhaps advocate violence or anything like that. But if a man gets up, as hundreds and thousands will during the coming campaign, and criticizes legislation that has been placed on the statute books by this or perhaps the preceding government, surely he Should not be liable to a penalty or to imprisonment for doing so. The minister says the commission have never exercised that power, but I do not regard that as a satisfactory answer at all. We might pass a law providing that a man might be hanged for stealing; it might be said that no one ever is hanged for stealing, but that would not be a
sufficient excuse. I .maintain that this power should not be in the hands of the commission at all.
Are these the regulations of the commission?
Yes.

Would it not be very easy for the minister to see that this regulation is removed? So long as the regulation is there it is quite possible that the man in charge of radio broadcasting, that is to say Mr. Charlesworth, might decide to live up to the regulations, as he should. If he lives up to them and carries out the intent of that provision then any opposition member of this house would be barred from speaking against any legislation that has been enacted by the government. Since that is the case I think in fairness, and in order to protect the right of freedom of expression, the minister should see that this restriction is removed from the regulations of the commission. I believe there was some difficulty last year in British Columbia, where a political organization was deprived of the right to use the radio because they were delivering political speeches which evidently were not satisfactory to certain persons who were opposed to them. I believe in that case the regulations were carried out. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the minister pledge himself to this committee-
No; let the minister present the amended regulations to the house.

He should either present the regulations to the house or pledge himself to the committee that at least this regulation will be eliminated from the rules governing broadcasting in Canada. I agree that there may be times when a broadcasting station may be justified in barring certain types of radio speeches. I need not mention the types that probably would be objectionable, but I think when it comes to a fair discussion of political questions and a fair expression of opinion there should be no limit to the use of the radio in this country.

Mr. Chairman, as a supporter of public ownership may I say that if the radio commission is a sample of public ownership the sooner it dies a natural death the better it will be for this country. I sat in opposition when a royal commission was appointed, consisting of Sir John Aird and others, to go into this question; that was about the time of the Beauhamois deal. They went all over the world; they even went to Japan, and in their report they recommended the appointment of such a commission. Last

year we voted $1,250,000 for the radio commission, which represented an increase of $250,000 over the previous year.
There is a great deal of dissatisfaction with the administration of this commission and with the gentlemen who are members of it. I was listening to the radio last Sunday evening; I was receiving an Anglican service from St. Simon's church, Toronto, from seven to eight o'clock. The prayer before the recessional hymn was written by the great Archbishop Cranmer, who was burned at the stake during the reformation; then, in the midst of the singing, the station switched off the church service and switched on a cocoa advertisement, a Yankee tobacco advertisement and other programs of that kind. Where does the Lord's Day Act come in? It would be a good thing for the people of Canada if this particular kind of public ownership were abolished; even if it meant an increase in licence fees it would be better for us, if we could get rid of some of the objectionable advertising that is being broadcast day after day. We have heard a good deal about the new deal. I know of no agency that is doing more to Americanize the people of Canada than this same radio commission. This commission was set up by a Liberal government., and in the Toronto district the employees are very largely Liberals. What they know about announcing is beyond me; I do not know where they obtained their experience. If the minister wants to have public ownership let him have real public ownership and give the people of this country radio service at cost. Let the people pay for it, and then perhaps we will not have to listen to the jazz that is broadcast night and day, winter and summer. Upon my word, as a Conservative I am surprised at what is heard over the radio, and even at what appears in the newspapers, in connection with politics, sports and everything else. The morning papers of Toronto carry about a page of American baseball news and about half a column of news about the House of Commons. The evening papers contain a few lines more. I would say in connection with this radio question that we have to go to the old country to see what is being done. I could tell you what the British Broadcasting Corporation did with the Baldwin government in 1924, 1925 and 1926; they put them out of office. Protests were received from Italy, Poland and other countries as to the political propaganda which was waged against Italy by the British Broadcasting Corporation. If we wish to continue as a Conservative party the people on the treasury

benches will have to take steps to put the brakes on the radio commission before the election.

have been issued by the department since the radio commission came into existence?

We have issued1 74
private licences for radio stations.
How many were there when the commission was established?

I am not informed
as to that.

I am informed that there
were only 49 when the commission was established. On the other hand we have established hardly any nationally owned stations, although that was the purpose behind the formation of the commission. The fact is however that we have immensely increased the number of private licences for radio broadcasting stations.

In what position would the
government be if at some future time it attempted to nationalize the broadcasting services? How would they take over the privately owned! stations?

Under the act the
radio commission has power to expropriate privately owned stations. I would refer the hon._ member to section 11 of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act.

In order to take over
privately owned stations upon what basis would the government have to proceed to undertake expropriation proceedings? What compensation would be expected?

Section 12 of the act covers the point:
The compensation payable in respect of the taking of any property so vested in the commission or of any interest therein or of lands injuriously affected by the construction of the undertakings or works shall be ascertained in accordance with the provisions of the Expropriation Act, and for that purpose the Attorney General of Canada may file an information in the Exchequer court on behalf of the commission-
And so on. In the event of there being no agreement between the owner and the government the exchequer court will pass on the amount of compensation.

that. If it comes to arbitration I am wondering if we will have to pay anything for that which is commonly described as goodwill?

anything would have to be paid for goodwill because the owners of stations have no vested rights in the channels. The licence is for a period of only six months, and may be withdrawn at the end of that time.

If such a matter were
referred to the exchequer court and that court were empowered to determine as to whether or not there may be any goodwill in the station taken over by the government, is there anything in the licence granted by the government to the private broadcasting stations which distinctly states that in the event of the government expropriating stations nothing will be paid for goodwill?

There is no such
provision in the licence because the departr-ment contends it is not necessary as such licence is issued for only six months.

I know that these matters
have been interpreted by courts on other occasions. Annual renewals almost assume the proportion of vested rights. Sometimes courts uphold such rights, and I have known of large amounts being spent in arbitration proceedings. In other words, if we grant privileges to these private companies and the time comes when we have to take over the stations we may have to pay a very heavy sum by way of damages for the privileges we are now granting. I have an objection to the granting of so many private licences, and when they are reissued I believe a clause ought to be inserted stating definitely and explicitly the conditions under which the licences are granted to the private broadcasting stations.

I should like to support
the observations of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I have a distinct recollection that during the proceedings of the original committee which sat in 1932, the matter was very fully discussed, and it was agreed at that time that if any private stations were expropriated or purchased by the government there was not to be any compensation for so-called goodwill of any concerns erecting private broadcasting stations in the future. There was a very clear understanding that they could not expect compensation for goodwill if at a later time they were expropriated by the government. I think the government should be sure it does not enter into any contract through which later on it might be compelled by court process to pay for goodwill.

I believe the point
is covered by section 13 of the act.
I hope it is.

I shall read the
section:
13 (1) In determining the compensation to be paid no allowance shall be made for the value of a licence terminated by the taking of any private station and no person shall be deemed to have any proprietary right in any channel heretofore or hereafter allotted, and no person shall be entitled to any compensation by reason of the cancellation of the allotment of a channel or by reason of the allotment of a new channel in substitution therefor.

Natural Products Marketing Act, 1934, $545,500.

The other night when the
minister was speaking on this vote he told us that there were certain schemes that had not been acted upon, not being considered expedient. One was the butter export scheme. Can he tell us why this one was not considered desirable in the public interest?

The hon. member wrote me a

I have not a copy of the scheme before me, but if the hon. member will let it stand I will get the information as soon as the officials come in.

The next matter I want to
speak about is the British Columbia sheep breeders' scheme, which was rejected because the principal market for the regulated product was within the area of production. The minister's letter states:
This scheme has now been gazetted under the Natural Products Marketing Act (British Columbia) 1934, and has been presented) to the Dominion Marketing Board for supplementary powers' under the federal act. It is receiving consideration by the board.
It is receiving consideration by the board. I have a statement from the British Columbia newspapers which says:
Activities of the British Columbia sheep marketing board have been suspended at Victoria. A letter was sent to Hon. K. C. Macdonald, Minister of Agriculture, over the week end, from the Salt Spring Island sheep breeders' association, asking for delay and calling the minister's attention to the fact that less than five per cent of the actual sheep breeders of the province have yet expressed am opinion for or against th-e marketing scheme.
The minister tells us that the scheme has been approved by the local marketing board of British Columbia and is now before the dominion board for consideration. Is he aware of this other statement, that only five per cent of the actual sheep breeders have expressed an opinion? Is it a desirable system whereby schemes can pass the provincial board and come to the dominion board for consideration, when only five per cent of the people have been consulted?
[Mr. Rhodes.1

Certain things were included in the scheme which the dominion board doubted could be put into effect. My information is that a long wire has been sent to the proponents of the scheme, asking them to give it further consideration.
The provincial government has been asked to give further consideration?
Not the provincial government but the British Columbia sheep-breeders' Association, those submitting the scheme.

But I understood the minister to say that it was rejected because the market for the regulated product was within the area of production. It was then taken* up under the British Columbia act and O.K.'d and sent to the dominion board. It is now being considered by the dominion board, but I say that it should not be considered favourably if only five per cent of the people have been consulted.
That matter will be taken into consideration. The scheme is under consideration by the dominion board.

There is another point. In
connection with the British Columbia salt fish board, it appears that this has been formed as I am afraid so many of these boards will be formed, and it is one of the greatest weaknesses of the act. We did not follow the British system, which is confined exclusively to producers. Under our act we very unwisely, as I thought at the time, extended the provisions to take in middlemen, marketers, or even marketers alone can start a scheme; and that opens the door to what will prove in the future to be a great deal of trouble. I do not mind prophesying now that within eighteen months it will be discovered, not in connection with this board but in some of these schemes, that the manipulation of a few small groups of middlemen, the men engaged in marketing the product, will lend itself to a gross misuse of their powers. If it had been confined to producers it would have been very different. I have not a word to say about the management of this British Columbia salt fish board; no doubt they are all right. But I want to make this other point. It appears that no fisherman is on the local board, which is composed entirely of men engaged in the marketing end. Now the whole purpose of the marketing act, if it had any precise object in view, was to benefit the primary producers. Here we are dealing with the fish industry, and surely the primary producers are those who catch the fish. Yet

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
there are none of these on the board. The statement is made that the operation of the scheme has been satisfactory and profitable, but profitable to whom? To the men who compose the board and not to the fishermen, who have not had an opportunity to benefit, not having been represented on the board. The scheme was put into effect after the fish were all caught. I point this out as an illustration of the way in which we are getting away from the real object of the act and drifting along the lines I predicted a year ago, with the result that certain schemes are entirely in the hands of middlemen.
There is one other point I wish to make -it was brought home forcibly to us in British Columbia, and it appears to me to strike at the very crux, the whole existence of the act- and it is this: a local board could be formed and organized to handle a certain product in a certain area; then it presently discovered, as we found out in British Columbia, that it was not possible to prevent the particular product, namely, potatoes, from being shipped in from an outside district. The result was that the whole scheme was absolutely abortive. I appealed to the British Columbia government and asked what was their interpretation and their proposed remedy. I pointed out that we had a potato board proposing to operate on Vancouver island, and I suspected that the scheme would be ruined because potatoes could1 and would be imported from any area outside that designated, in other words, from the neighbourhood of Lulu island where they grow a large quantity to the acre of an inferior quality. The answer I received from the British Columbia marketing board was that the only way to deal with the situation was to get the two districts to agree not to ship into each other's territory. That sounded very nice, but naturally it would not work. Vancouver island, which was an importing area, which had a shortage, would not ship into an area of cheap production, but the area of cheap production would not agree voluntarily and1 with no recompense to stop shipping its product into a considerable market on Vancouver island. The result was that this particular scheme fell flat. The area was then enlarged to take in both Vancouver island and a considerable section of the lower mainland. It was then discovered that potatoes outside that area were being shipped in quite legitimately, not bootlegged, and without any restrictions as to price, quantity or marketing regulations. In other words the local scheme is threatened with complete failure.
The same thing is likely to happen, and I think it was indicated it would1 happen, in 92582-214^
connection with the sheep and lamb board proposed in British Columbia. It was all very nice as long as we regulated our own lambs, but we could not stop the Alberta lambs from being shipped in and flooding the market. The whole purpose of the act seems to be dissipated on account of inability to control the product from areas outside that designated by the board. The remedy would appear to be to have given the local board power to deal with all produce of that particular variety, either grown or imported into the area. I submit that to the minister and I would like his opinion whether that would not be advisable or at least whether it will not be highly necessary, or else all these boards will be just a joke. What is the use of regulating a large area of a province when another part of that province or another province can ship in stuff to the total destruction of the market? These boards cost money to handle, fifty cents or a dollar a ton, and what is to be the benefit? The minister will either have to give the local board power to handle imported as well as locally grown stuff or else to explain of what use the board is.

This was one of the most troublesome problems we had in developing this legislation. The particular scheme to which the hon. member refe'rs was given- very serious consideration by the dominion marketing board, and it was first thought that the only solution in connection with this one particular scheme was that the area should have been in the first place large enough to get over those local conditions. The hon. member realizes that if an attempt were made to restrict areas so that products could not be shipped under any conditions into certain areas where products were being regulated, that would be equivalent to setting up a prohibitive tariff wall around that area. That would create a complicated and almost impossible situation. It was the purpose when this act was brought before the house and enacted, and it still is, that the areas would be sufficiently large to get over the difficulty that has been mentioned. But I can again assure the hon. member that the government had a full appreciation of those difficulties, and they probably gave us more concern than anything else in connection with the marketing board. We have been trying to devise some amendment to the act that will to some extent overcome this.
Will the legislation be introduced this year?

I would not be prepared yet to go that far.

and seven limited companies produce the balance of the tobacco. The minister said that I might make some remarks at this time with regard to the administration of the Customs Act. I am glad to see both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Matthews) in the chamber. The Minister of Finance determines the amount of taxation and then the Minister of National Revenue and his department undertake to collect that taxation. We have reason to believe that sometimes the Depart-
Excise Act Amendment

ment of National Revenue is so much interested in obtaining the last cent of revenue that it violates the spirit of the Customs Act We had an illustration of this two or three years ago in connection with the duty on repair parts for farm implements. I want to bring that matter again to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue and also to take up another matter to which I referred the other day when speaking on the motion to go into supply. At that time I referred to the complaint which had been made in connection with the imposing of a dump duty upon certain fishermen's supplies which came in free of duty. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) expressed the opinion that that had reference to goods coming in from Japan, but I hold in my hand a copy of a letter which indicates that the complaint was made in connection with goods coming in from Norway. This letter, which is addressed to the Minister of National Revenue, reads:
The representatives of your local customs called on us to-day in connection with the importation of nets and rope from Norway, lit is our understanding that you propose assessing dump duty on nets imported from Norway, and which .are o-n the free list. We take some credit for stirring up this trouble between Japan and your government, as we wrote some of our principals there, explaining the difficulty of importing goods from them on account of your unreasonable dump duty. It is our understanding that the balance of trade between Norway and Canada is in favour of ourselves. Therefore we propose advising Norway of the rate, so that they, like Japan, may take steps to convince your government that they cannot carry on a one-sided trade.
We trust that you will not be sufficiently blind to the interests of Canada to put a dump duty on goods that are admitted free, because similar goods are made in Canada. Our fishermen are compelled to sell their goods on the markets of the world and take the world price. They cannot exist and pay the high protected prices in, existence in Canada. If the Canadian manufacturers are desirous of selling goods to those who have to sell their wares in world markets, then they must be prepared to get their prices down to those of the world.
Personally, I have no immediate interest in the fishermen, but fishermen are one class of primary producers in Canada, and the interests of Canada as well as of the primary producers themselves demand that the implements of production, whatever they may be, be admitted at the lowest possible rate. And since these articles used by fishermen are put on the free list, it would seem to be a violation of the spirit and intent of the act that a dumping duty should be imposed. I call attention also to the question of repairs on agricultural implements. So far as the general run of agricultural implements are concerned,

that was satisfactorily adjusted two years ago when the Minister of Finance placed these repairs on the list at the duties prevailing before the tariff was raised in the fall of 1930. There is, however, one implement on which the ruling of the Department of National Revenue is by no means satisfactory; I refer to the situation in regard to. repairs for tractors. Item 409m reads:
Internal combustion traction engines for farm purposes, valued at not more than fourteen hundred dollars each; traction attachments designed and imported to be combined with automobiles in Canada for use as traction engines for farm purposes; and complete parte of all tbe foregoing: Free.
It was the understanding that repair parts for implements should come in at the rate of duty that prevailed on repairs before the tariff was raised in the fall of 1930. Now in regard to these repair parts for tractors, I have already called the attention of the house to the fact that the department has ruled that these repairs, constituting bolts, nuts, washers, rivets, lock washers, screws-copper or brass-* tractor gaskets, cork gaskets, copper gaskets, asbestos gaskets and paper gaskets, shall now be charged a duty of from 25 to 35 per cent. A bulletin of the department, issued November 12, 1927, reads:
Declares that any article which constitutes a part of a part, provided it requires no further fabrication and is not adapted for any other use, is entitled to entry as a complete part.
I submit that these words "and is not adapted for any other use" should be stricken out. It is perfectly true in regard to engines that many of the bolts, for instance, which are used on engines, whether steam or gasoline, may be used for something else; but it is also true that 'bolts are made especially suited for a particular engine and only that particular bolt can be used in that part of the engine, though undoubtedly, as I say, a bolt may be used for some other purpose. If the department bases its ruling on the fact that these bolts may be used for some other purpose, then I suggest that that clause be stricken out, "and is not adapted for any other use." To the users of engines this is an important consideration. The companies that handle these supplies have to keep a large stock on hand in order to meet the necessities of the farmers, because these engine Tepairs are often needed at very short notice and it would not be possible for the wholesaler in Winnipeg to get them readily from the manufacturer in the United States. I submit that the Minister of National Revenue should give this subject con-

sideration and instruct the officers of his department to apply the law according to what we believe was the spirit and intent of it when it was passed under the leadership of the Minister of Finance.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. C. MATTHEWS (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
I am very glad the hon. member has called my attentiop to the matter and I will endeavour to reply with the information at my command. The first complaint has reference to representations made direct to the department on May 22 last, by a firm of ship chandlers in Prince Rupert, I believe, to the effect that currency dump should not apply to importations from Norway of fishermen's ropes and nets which are entitled to free entry from all countries under tariff item 682. I may say that order in council P.C. 2549, passed on October 10, 1931, provided, in respect of goods imported from countries having depreciated currencies, that the value for duty of such goods should be computed in accordance with currency values as proclaimed by the governor in council under section 55 of the Customs Act. This order in council, which also provided for the collection of special duty under section 6 of the customs tariff, in cases where the selling price to the purchaser in Canada was for a lesser amount than the value for duty as computed in the manner stated, applies to all currencies whose values have been proclaimed and which have become depreciated. The proclaimed value of the Norwegian krone is 26-80 cents in Canadian currency and at the present time it has depreciated to a value of about 24-75 cents. In this instance therefore the currency dump is practically negligible. In any event, I am informed that there are very few importations of fishermen's ropes and nets from Norway.
Section 6 of the customs tariff provides for a special duty in respect of goods of a class or kind produced in Canada, although the goods are not otherwise dutiable; and in this connection fishing nets and netting, whether of linen or of cotton, with the exception of salmon gill nets with double knots, are regarded by the department as of a class or kind produced in Canada and are therefore liable to special or dumping duty.
Accordingly it will be apparent that in this particular instance there has been no discrimination whatever against fish nets from Norway. The correspondence from the Prince Rupert company is now receiving consideration by the department and an adequate reply will be sent to them direct in due course.
With regard to the second complaint made by my hon. friend, which has reference to the tariff status of repair parts for farm traction engines, I may say that so far as anyone at present on the staff of the Department of National Revenue can remember, it has always been ruled and held for customs tariff purposes that a complete part is precisely as defined in appraisers bulletin 3383 of November 12, 1027, which was quoted by my hon. friend and which reads as follows:
That any article which constitutes a part of a part, provided it requires no further fabrication and is not adapted for any other use, is entitled to entry as a complete part.
The decision of the board of customs as contained in appraisers bulletin 3383 merely confirmed this ruling on appeal.
For the information of my hon. friend I may say that the department classifies as complete parts such articles as cylinder head gaskets, manifold gaskets, oil pan gaskets and other special gaskets irrespective of the material of which they are made, which are obviously specially designed for use only as parts of a particular traction engine, and admits the same to duty free entry under tariff item 409m when for use on traction engines for farm purposes, valued at not more than SI,400 each. The department also deals similarly with washers so-called, of special shape, which are specially designed for use as parts of tractors and which do not lend themselves to other use. However, bolts, nuts, washers, rivets and screws which are adapted for other uses cannot be classified by the department as "complete parts" in view of the decision of the former board of customs. I think this answer will cover the point raised by my hon. friend.
Mr. BRXJW1N: According to my information tractor gaskets, cork, are being charged at 20 per cent, and, copper, at 30 per cent. We all know that a gasket for a tractor is made for one particular type of engine and cannot be used for any other. That is a matter of common knowledge.

I cannot quite understand why the minister wants to incorporate the bargain in legislation, when he could do it by agreement. On a former occasion he reduced the excise on cigarettes. I think my hon. friend
will be the first to admit it would be a very difficult matter to call into conference representatives of the liquor commissions of nine different provinces and consult them in advance in respect to a reduction in tariff involving as it does revenue running into hundreds of thousands of dollars. As a matter of fact it is a practical impossibility, having regard to the secrecy which of necessity must surround a change in tariff. The result is that the liquor commissions receive the information through the press, and the only lever we could keep in our hands was to insert a provision such as obtains in the clause in question. This was an idea of my own; I think it will work; the purpose is plain and I believe it would be worth while to give it a year's trial.

I do not want to prolong the discussion, but I think the plan would work without this clause. The principle of introducing a bargain of this kind

I would like to refer to the
question of nets and twine for fishermen. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) read a letter from Prince Rupert, and the minister replied that the difference was due to depreciated currency of Norway. He informed the committee, quite correctly of course, that the depreciation was so small in the case of that country that there would not be much increase of tax. But that does not apply to Japan. As the minister knows, the depreciation of Japanese currency is very great. Let me give a specific case which came to my notice when I was in Nova Scotia during the recess. I had sufficient time to go around and visit some of my fishermen friends, not in my own constituency but in another. The afternoon I called on one man he was engaged in putting a piece in his fish trap, and I noticed that he had some very nice twine. I asked him where he got it, he told me it came from Japan. I asked him what it cost, he told me it cost him twenty cents a pound, but, he said, the duty on it was more than the cost of the twine. I asked him how much he paid for the twine, and he said he paid S600, but that the tax was S630. This was a fisherman, a man who had to go out in the ocean and risk his gear and sometimes his life to earn his livelihood. This government, or the minister of the department, made this poor man pay S30 more than the cost of the twine in duty; the twine cost him S600 and he had to pay at the customs house S630 in duty before he could get delivery. That seems to me an outrage,
especially in view of the condition of the fishing industry in this country. I was always opposed to dumping duties; I believe in free trade. The people should not have to pay customs duties, whether dumping or otherwise, and I say it is an outrage to the fishermen of this country that they should have to pay $630 tax on $600 worth of twine.

My hon. friend will
appreciate that the dumping duty of which he speaks is due entirely to the depreciated currency of Japan. The par value of the yen is 49'89 cents, and the proclaimed value for duty purposes is the same, but the present value of the yen is only about 28-90 cents. That is where the difference comes in, and the dumping duty. The hon. member will also appreciate that this department merely administers the law in collecting the duty.

Quite right, but it is a very
bad law when a poor fisherman, finding a place where he can get some cheap twine, imports it and has to pay $630 on a $600 article, whether it be dumping duty or whatever you like to call it. I say the law should be changed. It is not fair to the industry or to the individual, and in my opinion it is not right.

I wish to make a few remarks on some statements that were made by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). The hon. member for Northumberland. Ont. (Mr. Fraser) characterized that speech very well. I must admit it was a noble and courageous effort on the part of the hon. member to respond to the SOS call of the

Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir). But while it was a noble effort we cannot say much in praise of the material of his speech. I shall not deal with it at any length, but there is one sentence to which I call attention. He said, as reported on page 3300 of Hansard:
Mr. Rowe: Danish bacon was being sold in our western stores, and our barley was being used to fatten Danish hogs.
I take the first part of that statement, that Danish bacon was being sold in our western stares. Perhaps the hon. member made that statement in good faith; sometimes men repeat so often statements they have heard that they come to believe them. It is said of George IV that he declared so often that he had been present at the battle of Waterloo that he came to believe he had been, and when the Duke of Wellington was asked about it by the king he replied "Well, I have heard your Majesty say so." This is one of the loose statements which Conservative speakers have been making all through the country. Similar loose statements have been made in regard to the tariff in many respects. I took occasion to look up the trade returns of Canada, and I found that from 1923 to 1930 there is no record of a single pound of Danish bacon being imported. So much for the first part of that statement. Then, the hon. member said that our barley was being used to fatten Danish hogs. This was just one of the loose statements made by the hon. member in the course of the rambling speech he made in response to the SOS call of the Minister of Agriculture. We know the minister needed his help very badly, as he needs it again to-night. So I just want to call the attention of the house and the country to the fact that, according to the trade returns, that statement will not bear investigation.
In response to the hon. member for Lisgar, I should like to say that I did not receive an SOS call from the Minister of Agriculture.
Then your effort is still more worthy of commendation.

I thank my good friend1, but that is an evidence of his own loose statements. The Minister of Agriculture does not need any help from me; as a matter of fact I asked if he would mind if I made a few remarks. I regret that due to the interruptions from the other side I perhaps did not make the remarks I intended to make when I rose. It is not my intention to speak at any length tonight; I know it is not the desire of the hon. members who interrupted so vociferously the other evening that I should do so.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Through you, Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. gentleman whether this is the same speech he made the other evening, or a new speech?
Through you, Mr. Chairman, I might tell my genial friend that the policy of his party for the last twenty years has been to wait and see, and I might suggest that he follow that policy still.
It would have cost less if your government had done the same thing.

Yes, another voice suggesting that we should have done the same thing. Thank God we did not, so far as Canada is concerned. I do not propose that the hon. member for Lisgar or anyone else shall direct me away from what I propose to say. I know very well that I could find many loose statements that have been made by the hon. member; in fact, I remember his saying, when he sat in the far corner of the house, what little regard he had for either of the major parties.
You never did.

Even now, apparently, the
people of his own riding doubt his sincerity when he talks there about being a Progressive.

Will the hon. gentleman
just permit me and my constituents to settle that matter between ourselves?
They have settled it.

According to all reports the matter is already settled. I know that my hon. friend came here with good intentions, as I said the other night. He did not intend to make any reckless statements; he came here intending to assist in the cooperative marketing of agricultural products, which was the object of the organization he represented. In the first place the farmers of old Ontario organized in order to help the farmers to get a fair price for their products, and it was through the organization that followed that first step that the hon. member for Lisgar and other hon. members first came to this parliament. But when he saw the advantage of getting back to his first love he not only made reckless statements, he recklessly disregarded his second love and came nearer the front benches of the party to which he now belongs.
It was no reckless statement the other night when I said that our overseas markets were lost before this government came into power. I say that the Natural Products Marketing Act is more fundamentally as-

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
sociated with our agricultural prosperity than perhaps those on this side of the house who drafted the act can imagine, certainly much more than those who sit to your left appreciate. I know the leaders in every line of Canadian enterprise and activity have stated repeatedly that unless agriculture is brought back to prosperity there is little hope for the future, and I will say that I believe hon. gentlemen opposite are in agreement with that statement. One thing is sure; only through the wise and careful marketing of our products can we hope to receive the best return for what we produce. I think that is generally acknowledged. I have stated before in this house, Mr. Chairman, and I repeat-and this is no reckless or ill-considered statement-that we had ten years of an absolutely lopsided agricultural policy in this country from 1920 to 1030, with little regard paid to marketing conditions. That was so much the case that the sound development of Canadian agriculture almost disappeared. I know it is true that we marketed much more wheat, but undoubtedly if we had possessed a natural products marketing act in 1920 and had exercised the powers now contained in that act we would have preserved some of our overseas markets which were lost when hon. gentlemen who sit opposite were in power.
I think everyone will appreciate that if any phase of Canadian agriculture should be developed on a sound basis it is the careful and systematic sale of the products of mixed farming. I know that for years my friends from western Canada, both in this parliament and on the hustings, have criticized this government for their policy of protection. 1 can remember, some eight or ten years ago, istening to the wheat growers tell us in this nouse that we should have free trade or at least a lower tariff on farm implements, and I rather admired the zeal of my hon. friend from Lisgar to-night in requesting that even the nuts, bolts and screws that go to make up a binder should be put on the free list. But may I remind him that when the tariff on farm implements was reduced before 1930 we paid more for those implements than we had paid before the change was made. May I remind him also that the tariffs have been raised since that time but we pay less for these implements, so apparently the tariff has very little bearing on the price paid.

Well, we have an advantage in the British market of SI 25 in connection with our apples and we enjoy an advantage in other lines as well, but I repeat-I have said this before and I repeat it now by way of emphasis- that it is absolutely necessary that Canadian agriculture should be made prosperous once more if Canadian industry generally is to return to prosperity. And if this is to come about we must have an increase in agricultural prices. I believe that under the act we have the power to set aside a stabilization fund for the purpose of disposing of our surplus products in the export market. I should like to say, in reply to the statement of the minister concerning the act to which he referred1 a moment ago, that the penalties imposed under that act bring it into exactly the same category as the Weights and Measures Act; it is a case of standardizing and selling the consumer products of a certain quality. That is an entirely different feature; that is an entirely different purpose from the Natural Products Marketing Act. In that case, if you sell a man a rotten apple you are fined. If he wants to buy a Spy and you try to sell him a Ben Davis, naturally you will be fined, just the same as if you give a man a counterfeit dollar you will be fined. That bill is in exactly the same category as the Weights and Measures Act, with which we all agree. With that principle I entirely agree, as I always have agreed, but the penalties under the Natural Products Marketing Act are entirely different. These penalties are to be applied in order to try to make a person do what you cannot make him do. I quite realize, as the minister has said, that in all these schemes some people break away; in this case you are going to apply penalties to a minority, in the way of fines and gaol sentences, in order to force the minority to do as the majority desire. As I said the other night, that was what we tried to do in connection with liquor and narcotics, and we found that it could not be done. Now you are trying to do it in connection with food products.
In the first place, Mr. Chairman, there are four distinct features to this act. There are the penalty clauses; there is the removal from the House of Commons of the right to regulate exports and imports; there is the clause which places in the hands of a board not under the control of the parliament of Canada the right of taxation, and in the fourth place you put in the hands of that board rights which should be and are under the sole jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. Those are the objectionable features of the act. If the act were so drafted that it could be used to assist the farmers instead of trying to do these things you cannot do, it would be a different proposition; as I have already said, cooperation is all right.
I should like to mention another point in connection with this act. A moment ago the Minister of Agriculture said that it did not provide for monopolies or for price fixing I agree with only part of what the minister has said. I have in mind the jam scheme. Under that scheme, which I believe has been adopted by the federal board, the price of jam has been fixed; specifically, the price of marmalade, which is made out of an imported product-Jaffa, Spanish or Italian oranges- has been increased to the Canadian consumer by neatly one hundred per cent. If any producers are to benefit under that scheme it can only be the Arabs or Jews of Jerusalem, the Spaniards of Spain or the Italians of Italy. Unquestionably, there is the right of monopoly under this act.
I should like to return to the fact that public moneys are being spent under the jurisdiction of this board1 in an endeavour to coerce-or I might use the word "kid"

people into trying to do something they do not want to do. Just listen to this for a moment. In Alberta the sum of $584 was spent for broadcasting. Just imagine using a propagandist over a broadcasting station to tell the Alberta farmers how to raise chickens and how to sell eggs. That is the way the money is being spent. Then there is item after item for speakers. Imagine paying speakers to go out on the public platform to advocate a scheme such as this. I happen to know some of the speakers by name, and if I did not know any more about keeping chickens, raising hens, or producing eggs than some of the people on this list know I would go into the horse doctor business without any hesitation. That is the way this money has been spent. I want to be emphatic about this. Apparently, from this statement, that is the way it is intended to proceed in 1935 and spend $500,000 of the people's money. And let me repeat that this $500,000 will not be spent under the direction of people who have spent their lives in successful business, farming or otherwise. It will be spent under the direction of academic minds and a lot of people who think they know more about other people's business than they do know. If you think the basic producers, whom the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe said to-night are toiling sixteen hours a day in order to get enough money to pay the sugar tax, their other taxes and the interest on their mortgages, are going to let any white collar, ten thousand dollar a year men, with shining cars, run around this country and broadcast over expensive stations, telling them how to get more eggs out of a hen, you are very much mistaken. I suggest to the minister that before this item passes he should carefully consider how this money is to be spent. He should be very careful before spending half a million dollars of the money of the taxpayers in trying to do impossible, uneconomic things that have been proven wrong from the Malay straits to south of
